notes.22:30: Greek elysen ("unbound") refers to removing Paul's chains rather than freeing him from Roman custody.
notes.23:8: Greek amphotera literally means "both," either grouping "angel" and "spirit" together as one category alongside "resurrection" or reflecting Koine Greek usage meaning "all of them."
notes.23:9: The Greek sentence breaks off abruptly after "or an angel" (aposiopesis); later manuscripts add "let us not fight against God" to complete the clause.
notes.23:20: The critical text reads the singular participle mellon ("as though you were going to inquire"), attributing the pretext to the commander, whereas some manuscripts read plural forms referring to the Sanhedrin.
notes.23:23: The rare Greek term dexiolabos (literally "right-side taker," occurring only here in the New Testament) denotes a class of light-armed infantry, usually understood as spearmen or lancers.
notes.24:6: The earliest manuscripts lack the material traditionally numbered as verse 7 (with portions of verses 6 and 8) describing Lysias intervening by force; the Saints Greek Critical Text prints verse 7 within double brackets ⟦ ⟧ (shown as an additional verse). In the shorter text, "from him" in 24:8 refers directly to Paul.
notes.24:19: The Greek syntax breaks off abruptly (anacoluthon) after introducing "some Jews from Asia," shifting directly to the relative clause stating what they ought to have done.
notes.25:13: The critical text reads the aorist participle aspasamenoi rather than the future participle aspasomenoi of later manuscripts; in Hellenistic Greek an aorist participle after a verb of motion can express attendant circumstance or purpose.
notes.25:19: Greek deisidaimonia can mean either "religion" (neutral) or "superstition" (pejorative); addressing King Agrippa, Festus likely uses the term politely to mean "religion."
notes.25:21: Greek Sebastos is the standard equivalent of the Latin imperial title Augustus, referring here to Emperor Nero (also in 25:25).
notes.25:26: Literally "to the lord" (to kyrio), a Roman title (dominus) used here by a provincial governor referring to the emperor.
notes.26:11: The imperfect enagkazon ("I kept trying to force") is likely conative, describing repeated attempts to compel believers to blaspheme rather than necessarily succeeding.
notes.26:14: Greek te Hebraidi dialekto ("in the Hebrew dialect") commonly refers to Aramaic, the Semitic language spoken in first-century Judea, consistent with the form Saoul ("Saul").
notes.26:23: Greek ei (literally "whether") introduces the propositions at issue, and pathetos literally means "subject to suffering" or "destined to suffer."
notes.26:28: Greek en oligo can mean "in a short time" or "with little effort." The critical text reads poiesai (literally "to make," perhaps "to act the Christian" or "to make [me] a Christian"), which later manuscripts smooth to genesthai ("to become").
notes.27:9: "The Fast" refers to the Day of Atonement (Yom Kippur) in late September or October, after which open-sea navigation on the Mediterranean became hazardous.
notes.27:12: Literally "looking down the southwest wind and down the northwest wind"; scholars debate whether this describes a harbor opening toward the southwest and northwest, or toward the northeast and southeast (the direction in which those winds blow).
notes.27:17: "Lowered the gear" translates a general nautical term (skeuos) whose exact referent is debated, likely meaning either lowering the main sail and rigging or deploying a sea anchor to slow the ship's drift toward the Syrtis sandbanks.
notes.27:27: In first-century geography, "the Adriatic Sea" (ho Adrias) encompassed the central Mediterranean between Greece, Crete, Sicily, and Malta, not merely the modern Adriatic.
notes.27:41: The text reads simply "by the violence" (hypo tes bias); some later manuscripts add "of the waves," which is absent from the earliest witnesses followed here.
notes.28:2: Greek "barbaroi" (also in 28:4), a neutral term for non-Greek speakers—here the native Punic-speaking inhabitants of Malta—rather than "barbarians" in the modern sense.
notes.28:7: Literally "the first man of the island" (Greek "protos"), an official Roman-era title for the chief magistrate of Malta attested in local inscriptions.
notes.28:11: Greek "Dioskurois" (the Dioscuri), the mythological twin sons of Zeus—Castor and Pollux—regarded in antiquity as patron deities of sailors.
notes.28:13: The critical text reads "perielontes" ("having cast off" or "weighed anchor"); some manuscripts read "perielthontes" ("having sailed around" or "made a circuit").
notes.28:28: Verse 29 ("And when he had said these things, the Jews departed, having a great dispute among themselves") is absent from the earliest manuscripts; the Saints Greek Critical Text prints it in double brackets ⟦ ⟧.
